query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (HEA), sustained exposure to service-relevant thermal and mechanical loads can induce nanoscale compositional fluctuations (incipient local chemical ordering/decomposition) preferentially at grain boundaries. These nanoscale heterogeneities act as weak interfacial links that reduce toughness, even in the absence of the coarse grain-boundary segregation or large intermetallic precipitates typical of conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, single-phase, equimolar or near-equimolar HEA with a homogeneous microstructure and high ductility.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging combined with cyclic or constant mechanical loading to simulate prolonged service conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (within the upper range of anticipated service temperatures) and mechanical loading levels that approach but do not exceed the alloy’s yield stress, maintained over a prolonged time to allow for potential local chemical reordering.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale compositional fluctuations and the development of short-range ordered regions at or near grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation and mechanical stress provide the driving force for local chemical instability in the HEA’s high-entropy matrix, promoting incipient, nanoscale phase separation (or ordering) at intergranular regions that compromises grain-boundary cohesion without forming the large-scale, brittle precipitates seen in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial baseline, specimens subjected to the intervention will exhibit measurable decreases in toughness (e.g., lower fracture resistance, earlier crack initiation at grain boundaries) alongside the detection of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities at the boundaries (via high-resolution TEM/EDS or atom probe tomography). This behavior will differ from conventional alloys, where embrittlement is linked to macroscopic intergranular precipitates or segregation.
generation.baseline: The ductile, single-phase HEA microstructure as initially produced, without detectable nanoscale chemical heterogeneity at grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEAs that retain a compositionally complex, single-phase structure and are used under service conditions that involve moderate-to-high temperature exposure and sub-critical mechanical loading. It may not apply if the alloy composition or processing inadvertently promotes coarse precipitation or grain-boundary segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thermal or mechanical thresholds that trigger the nanoscale chemical fluctuations, as well as the quantitative relationship between the extent of these fluctuations and the decrease in toughness, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples from the identical single-phase HEA to serve as a controlled test set. Subject one set of samples to prolonged thermal aging and cyclic loading that mimic service conditions, while another set remains in the as-cast state as a control. Perform high-resolution microscopic and spectroscopic analyses (e.g., TEM with EDS mapping, atom probe tomography) on both sets to assess nanoscale chemical ordering at grain boundaries. Concurrently, carry out standardized fracture toughness and ductility tests on both sample sets.
measurements: Quantitative fracture toughness (or impact toughness) values.
Fracture surface analysis to identify crack initiation sites (grain boundaries vs. bulk).
High-resolution imaging and compositional mapping of grain boundaries to detect nanoscale chemical fluctuations or ordering.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to service-like thermal and mechanical loads do not show a statistically significant reduction in toughness compared to the baseline, or if no measurable nanoscale chemical heterogeneity is detected at the grain boundaries in degraded samples, the hypothesis would be falsified. Likewise, if such heterogeneities are observed without an associated decline in toughness, the hypothesized mechanism would be invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
